# How to Make a Clear Pros-and-Cons List When You're Stuck on a Big Decision

> **In short:** This guide walks you through a six-step method for laying out every angle of a tough choice — moving, job change, a big purchase — so the answer stops feeling foggy. All you need is paper, a notes app, or any AI assistant to brainstorm with.

Big decisions feel foggy because the reasons are tangled — money talks to time, time talks to family, and suddenly you're arguing with yourself in the shower. This guide gives you a six-step method to pull those reasons out of your head, lay them on paper, and see what your own thinking is trying to tell you. One honest note up front: a list won't make the decision for you. It makes the decision *visible*, which is what makes deciding possible.

## Before you start
- About 20–30 minutes of quiet time, ideally in one sitting.
- Something to write on — paper, a notes app, or a blank document.
- Optional: any AI assistant (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat) to help you brainstorm angles you might miss.

## Step 1 — Name the decision in one sentence
The first thing to do is write down exactly what you're deciding. Not "should I move?" but something sharper — a specific question stops your list from sliding around later.

Open your notes app or grab a piece of paper. At the top, write your decision as a single question. Read it out loud. If you can read it in one breath, it's clear enough. If it has "and" in it ("Should I move AND get a new job?"), split it into two questions — that's two decisions, not one. If you don't have a notes app open, any scrap of paper works; the method doesn't care what you write on.

💬 Example: *"Should I move from my current apartment to the one across town that costs $200 more per month?"*

You'll know it worked when you can point at your sentence and say, "That's what I'm actually trying to figure out." If you can't, the next steps won't help yet — so spend a few minutes tightening the question first.

## Step 2 — Brainstorm the angles that matter
Now you list everything that could change because of this decision. Don't filter, don't judge — just get it out of your head. Most "stuck" feelings come from having too many thoughts circling, not too few.

Set a 5-minute timer. Write every angle that comes to mind: money, time, family, health, career, sleep, friendships, stress, what you'd miss, what you'd gain. Short words are fine — "more commute", "less rent", "nearer to mom". If you have an AI assistant open, ask it for angles you might miss. If 5 minutes feels like too long, even 2 minutes of writing counts — start with whatever surfaces first.

💬 Example prompt for any AI assistant: *"I'm trying to decide whether to move to a new apartment that costs $200 more per month. What angles should I think about that I might be missing?"*

You'll know it worked when you have between 8 and 20 short notes on the page. Less than 8 usually means you're filtering too early. More than 25 can be trimmed later — having too much is the better problem.

## Step 3 — Turn your notes into a two-column table
Now shape the mess into something your eyes can scan. A simple table forces both sides to sit next to each other, which is the whole point of a pros-and-cons list.

Draw two columns. Label the left one **Stays the same (pros of NOT changing)** and the right one **Changes (pros of changing)**. Move each note from Step 2 into the column where it fits. Some notes will feel like they belong in both — pick the column where the feeling is stronger, or write it in both. If drawing a table feels awkward, just use two lists with the same headings at the top of each. The shape matters less than having both sides visible.

💬 Example: *"Save $200/month"* might go in **Stays the same** (keeping your current apartment means you keep saving). *"Shorter commute"* goes in **Changes** (the new place gives you that).

You'll know it worked when you can look at the table and see one side is longer than the other — or roughly equal. If one column is empty, you haven't thought the decision through yet; go back to Step 2.

## Step 4 — Give each item a weight, not just a count
Counting pros and cons treats every item as equal. But "save $200/month" and "be nearer to family" don't weigh the same in real life. Adding a simple weight makes your list honest instead of misleading.

Decide on three weights: **Low**, **Medium**, **High**. Low means "nice, but I could live without it." High means "this would change how I feel day-to-day." Go through your table and mark each item. If you're using a notes app, add a small symbol — ★ for High, ● for Medium, ○ for Low. If three weights feel like too many, two is fine: "matters" and "doesn't matter much".

💬 Example: *"Save $200/month"* might be Medium (helpful, but I'd adjust). *"Be nearer to mom during her recovery"* might be High (this affects her wellbeing and mine).

You'll know it worked when you can point at one or two High items and say, "Those are the real reasons I keep going back and forth." Often the decision was always about those two — the list just made it visible.

## Step 5 — Look for what the list is actually saying
Step away from the table for five minutes. Get water, stretch, look out a window. When you come back, read the table without trying to argue with it. Notice which column your eye lands on first. Notice which items you keep explaining away.

A useful question: *"If a friend showed me this table and asked for advice, what would I tell them?"* Write that sentence down. It's usually closer to your real answer than the answer you've been defending. If walking away feels like procrastinating, set a phone timer for 5 minutes — that's your "walk away."

💬 Example: After reading the table, you might write: *"If my friend showed me this list, I'd say the High-weight items — mom's recovery and my sleep — point to moving, even though saving money matters. The money isn't a High item because I'd find a way."*

You'll know it worked when you can write a one-sentence answer to your original question. You don't have to commit to it yet — just see if a sentence is there.

## Step 6 — Stress-test the answer with a future-you question
The last step protects you from choosing on impulse. A pros-and-cons list catches facts, but it can miss how you'll feel in six months. One question closes that gap.

Write down: *"It's six months from now. I made the choice my list pointed to. What's one thing I hope is true, and one thing I'm worried will be true?"* Answer both honestly. If the "worried" answer is small and manageable, the list is probably right. If the "worried" answer is something you couldn't live with, your list is missing a row — go back to Step 2. If you can't picture six months ahead, picture one month from now instead — same idea, smaller window.

💬 Example: *"In six months, I hope I'm sleeping better and visiting mom twice a week. I'm worried I'll miss my old neighborhood and feel lonely for the first month. The loneliness is real but temporary. The sleep and visits are ongoing."*

You'll know it worked when the "hoped for" sentence feels true and the "worried" sentence feels livable. That's your signal to act — or to wait one more week and let the feeling settle. Either is a real answer.

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** Listing only facts, not feelings. **Fix:** Add at least three feelings to your Step 2 brainstorm — *"I'd feel relieved," "I'd miss my morning walk," "I'd feel proud."* Facts don't decide big choices; feelings do.
- **Mistake:** Mixing two decisions into one list. **Fix:** If your question has "and" in it, split it. A pros-and-cons list for "move AND change jobs" hides which choice is actually pulling at you.
- **Mistake:** Treating the list as a verdict. **Fix:** A list is a thinking tool, not a judge. If your gut says something different from your table, the table is missing a row — go find it.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** This same method works for smaller choices too — buying a laptop, ending a hobby, agreeing to a holiday plan. The six steps shrink or stretch to fit the size of the decision.
- **For your work or business:** Use the method before saying yes to a project, a job offer, or a new tool. A 20-minute list often catches the regret a 20-minute chat would have missed.
- **If you're just getting started:** Try the method on something small first — a purchase under $100 — to learn how your own brain weighs things. The skill transfers to the bigger choices later.

## Try it now
Pick one decision you've been putting off for a week or more. Write it as a single sentence at the top of a blank page. Give yourself 20 minutes to walk through Steps 1 to 4 — don't try to decide yet, just build the table. The answer usually shows up while you're building it.
